papers.title_in_file: Scalable Parameter Design for Superconducting Quantum Circuits with Graph Neural Networks
papers.version_note: The text is arXiv:2411.16354v3 (24 Jul 2025): a 7-page letter plus a 13-page Supplementary Materials, 20 pages in all. The file name says 2024, the text is dated July 25, 2025. The record id says 2025.
papers.what_it_is: A letter proposing a graph-neural-network designer, trained through a supervised MLP evaluator of simulated crosstalk errors, that assigns qubit and coupler frequencies on superconducting-circuit graphs of up to about 870 qubits, compared in simulation against the Snake optimizer and two direct optimizers.

existing.note: Value is right. The sentence is in the Discussion on page 4 of the text layer, not page 5 as the stored anchor says (page 5 holds the reference list).
existing.value: The authors state that in future research additional error sources and variations between qubits may be taken into account, and that the evaluator may be trained using experimental data.
quotes: In the future research, additional error sources and variations between qubits may be taken into account, and the evaluator may be trained using experimental data
existing.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limit in the Discussion: further error sources, qubit-to-qubit variation and experimental training data are left to future work.
existing.reader_inference: Taken with the simulation-only setup, this means every number in the paper comes from simulated crosstalk and from an evaluator fitted to simulated data.

existing.note: Value is right as an abstract claim, but the paper limits it: the errors compared are those estimated by one trained MLP evaluator (not measured on hardware and not simulated at 870 qubits), all methods used that same evaluator on the same CPU, and the figures are averages over 30 random graphs per scale. The designer training time (about 2 days on an RTX 4090 GPU) is not in the 27 sec.
existing.value: The authors report that for superconducting quantum circuits of around 870 qubits, their GNNs-based algorithm achieves 51% of the errors produced by the state-of-the-art algorithm, with a time reduction from 90 min to 27 sec; the errors are those estimated by the trained evaluator, and all methods employ the same trained evaluator on the same CPU.

All four methods employ the same trained evaluator on the same i914900KF CPU.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, simulated and scored by the authors' own evaluator.
existing.reader_inference: The main text gives 0.0090 against 0.0178, a ratio of about 0.51, which agrees with the abstract. The comparison at 870 qubits is against Snake only; the other two optimizers were not run at that scale.

a designer unsupervisedly trained on medium-scale circuits for applying to large-scale ones

assertions.value: The authors state that the theory-inspired evaluator is trained using smaller datasets, with each training set containing only 30, 720 data points, corresponding to 61, 440, 000 quantum measurements, which is 1/40 of the training data required for the MLPs-based evaluator in the main text.
quotes: The theory-inspired evaluator is trained using smaller datasets, with each training set containing only 30, 720 data points, corresponding to 61, 440, 000 quantum measurements, which is 1/40 of the training data required for the MLPs-based evaluator in the main text.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's stated figure; its arithmetic does not close against the paper's own numbers (see reader inference).
assertions.reader_inference: Checks against the paper's own numbers do not reproduce 1/40. The main-text evaluator trains on 61, 440 points and this one on 30, 720, a ratio of 1/2. With the supplement's own cost per point (2 initial states x 20 durations x 100 repeats = 4000 measurements), 30, 720 points is 122, 880, 000 measurements, not 61, 440, 000. Flag for the coordinator.

assertions.value: The authors report that, with the theory-inspired evaluator, on circuits with approximately 870 qubits the GNNs-based designer achieves an error of 0.0085 within several seconds, whereas the Snake algorithm requires several minutes to reach an error of 0.0181, and that the designer achieves lower errors than Snake across all scales.
quotes: the GNNsbased designer achieves lower errors than the Snake algorithm across all SQEC scales.
on SQECs with approximately 870 qubits, the GNNs-based designer achieves an error of 0.0085 within several seconds, whereas the Snake algorithm requires several minutes to reach an error of 0.0181.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, scored by a second authors' evaluator.
assertions.reader_inference: The ratio 0.0085 / 0.0181 is about 0.47. Snake takes several minutes here but 90 minutes with the MLP evaluator, so the 90-minute figure depends on the evaluator's cost per call.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because the dimension of the Hilbert space exponentially scales with the number of qubits, the evaluation of designed circuits through numerical simulations is becoming a challenging task, which further complicates automated design towards large-scale quantum processors.
